title: How to Add Passkeys to an iOS and Android App
summary: Add passkeys to iOS and Android apps with Swift and Kotlin. Configure domain associations, implement registration and sign-in, and verify credentials securely on your server.
body_markdown:
A passkey is a public/private key pair scoped to one domain. Your app creates it through the platform credential API, the server keeps only the public key, and Face ID or a fingerprint does nothing more than let the device use the private key.


A common way this goes wrong: the button is wired up, the backend works on the web, and on a real phone nothing appears. There’s no system sheet, no log line, and often just a generic cancellation error.


The cause is almost always one of three things: the app-to-domain association, a mismatch between the server’s relying party ID and that domain, or verification logic the server never finished. This guide covers each piece on iOS (Swift) and Android (Kotlin), with the server work for each step. It assumes you’ve already decided in favour of passkeys (the[passwords-versus-passkeys trade-off](https://blog.openreplay.com/a-security-question--passwords-or-passkeys/) is covered elsewhere).


## Key Takeaways


- An app can create or use a passkey for a domain only when the app declares that domain and the domain publishes a file naming the app:` apple-app-site-association` with` webcredentials` on iOS, and` assetlinks.json` with` delegate_permission/common.get_login_creds` on Android.
- The relying party ID the server sends must be the domain hosting both association files, and changing it later leaves every existing passkey unusable.
- Apps distributed with Play App Signing must list Google’s app signing key fingerprint in` assetlinks.json` . If you list only the upload key, passkeys work in local builds and fail for store installs.
- The server decides whether a passkey is valid. It checks a single-use challenge, the origin (including Android’s` android:apk-key-hash:` origin), the rpId hash and the signature before it creates a session.
- Synced passkeys follow the user’s Apple or Google account, so your account security now depends partly on theirs. Keep a recovery path that doesn’t rely on the passkey.


## Is a Passkey the Same as Biometric Unlock?


A passkey is not fingerprint unlock. Face ID or a fingerprint only lets the device use a private key that was created for one domain and never leaves the device or the user’s synced keychain. The server holds the matching public key and checks a signature. It never sees any biometric data.


Local biometric gating is a different mechanism. There, the app unlocks a token it stored earlier, and the server has no cryptographic proof of anything. If that’s what you need,[biometric authentication in React Native](https://blog.openreplay.com/biometrics-authentication-in-android-and-ios-apps-with-react-native/) covers the setup. This guide doesn’t repeat it.


## Platform Association: The Step That Fails Silently


The relying party ID (rpId) your server sends must be the same domain that hosts both association files. The operating system checks both sides independently. The app lists the domain, and the domain publishes a file listing the app. If either side is wrong, the passkey sheet never appears, and neither platform tells the app why.


### iOS: webcredentials Entitlement and apple-app-site-association


Add the domain to the[Associated Domains entitlement](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/entitlements/com.apple.developer.associated-domains) with the` webcredentials` service:


```text
<  key  >  com.apple.developer.associated-domains  </  key  >
<  array  >
<  string  >  webcredentials:example.com  </  string  >
</  array  >
```


Serve this file, with no extension, at` https://example.com/.well-known/apple-app-site-association` . The app ID is your Team ID and bundle ID joined by a dot:


```text
{
"  webcredentials  "  : {
"  apps  "  : [  "  ABCDE12345.com.example.shop  "  ]
}
}
```


Apple’s[supporting associated domains guide](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/supporting-associated-domains) says the file must come over HTTPS with a trusted certificate, and the request must not redirect. Because the file has no extension, many static hosts and object stores serve it with a generic binary content type, so set the type explicitly:


```text
location   =   /.well-known/apple-app-site-association   {
default_type application/json;
}
```


```text
curl   -sI   https://example.com/.well-known/apple-app-site-association   |   grep   -i   content-type
# expect: content-type: application/json
```


Devices don’t fetch this file from your server. They read a copy that Apple’s CDN fetches and caches. Apple’s documentation says the CDN requests the file within about 24 hours, and installed devices check for an updated copy roughly once a week. A corrected file therefore takes time to reach installed apps: the CDN has to re-fetch it first, and then each device picks it up on install, on update, or at its next weekly check. If the file was broken when the CDN fetched it, the CDN caches that broken result too. For development, use` webcredentials:example.com?mode=developer` and turn on Associated Domains Development under Settings › Developer on the device. The device then fetches the file directly from your domain. Remove the suffix before release, because release builds rely on the CDN copy.


### Android: assetlinks.json With get_login_creds


On Android,[Credential Manager passkeys need Digital Asset Links](https://developer.android.com/identity/credential-manager/prerequisites) at the rpId domain, served at` https://example.com/.well-known/assetlinks.json` :


```text
[
{
"  relation  "  : [  "  delegate_permission/common.get_login_creds  "  ],
"  target  "  : {
"  namespace  "  :   "  android_app  "  ,
"  package_name  "  :   "  com.example.shop  "  ,
"  sha256_cert_fingerprints  "  : [
"  <PLAY_APP_SIGNING_KEY_SHA256>  "  ,
"  <UPLOAD_KEY_SHA256>  "
]
}
}
]
```


List the fingerprint of any keystore you sign with:


```text
keytool   -list   -v   -keystore   release.keystore   -alias   release   |   grep   SHA256
```


If the app ships with[Play App Signing](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9842756) , Google re-signs it before delivery. The fingerprint that counts for store installs is the app signing key shown on the App signing page in Play Console. Listing only your local upload key is why passkeys work in debug builds and fail for users who installed from the store. Apps enrolled in Play’s quantum-ready hybrid signing have more than one app signing key, so add every SHA-256 fingerprint that page shows. Listing extra fingerprints does no harm.


### Pre-Flight Checks


Check How to verify Symptom if wrong


Content-Type` curl -sI` on the AASA URL No sheet on iOS


No redirects` curl -sI` returns 200, not 301/302 No sheet on either platform


Subdomain match Files served at the exact rpId host Works on web, fails in app


Play signing key Compare with Play Console’s App signing page Works in debug, fails from the store


Apple CDN copy Query the CDN URL below Old or broken file still in use


Subdomains don’t inherit association. The[Digital Asset Links specification](https://github.com/google/digitalassetlinks/blob/master/well-known/details.md) identifies a website by its scheme, exact host and port, so files at` www.example.com` do nothing for an rpId of` example.com` . Apple’s rule is the same: each subdomain needs its own` apple-app-site-association` file.


Both files can be checked without installing a build. The first URL returns what Apple’s CDN holds for your domain (Apple engineers use it for diagnosis; it isn’t a documented API). The second calls Google’s[statements.list endpoint](https://developers.google.com/digital-asset-links/reference/rest/v1/statements/list) :


```text
curl   https://app-site-association.cdn-apple.com/a/v1/example.com


curl   "  https://digitalassetlinks.googleapis.com/v1/statements:list?source.web.site=https://example.com&relation=delegate_permission/common.get_login_creds  "
```


A broken association throws no exception your crash reporter can catch. Session replay makes the pattern visible: a tap on “Sign in with passkey”, no system sheet, then the user switching to the password field. You can then filter those sessions by build and signing variant.


## How to Implement Passkeys: Registration


Passkey registration in a native app has three parts. The server creates options with a fresh challenge and` rp.id` set to the associated domain. The native API creates the credential. The server verifies the result and stores the public key and credential ID. The server’s options look like this:


```text
{
"  challenge  "  :   "  <base64url, random, single-use>  "  ,
"  rp  "  : {   "  id  "  :   "  example.com  "  ,   "  name  "  :   "  Example Shop  "   },
"  user  "  : {   "  id  "  :   "  <base64url user handle>  "  ,   "  name  "  :   "  ada@example.com  "  ,   "  displayName  "  :   "  Ada  "   },
"  pubKeyCredParams  "  : [{   "  type  "  :   "  public-key  "  ,   "  alg  "  :   -7   }],
"  authenticatorSelection  "  : {   "  residentKey  "  :   "  required  "  ,   "  userVerification  "  :   "  preferred  "   },
"  attestation  "  :   "  none  "  ,
"  excludeCredentials  "  : []
}
```


On iOS,[ASAuthorizationPlatformPublicKeyCredentialProvider](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/authenticationservices/asauthorizationplatformpublickeycredentialprovider) builds the request:


```text
let   provider   =   ASAuthorizationPlatformPublicKeyCredentialProvider  (  relyingPartyIdentifier  :   "  example.com  "  )
let   request   =   provider.  createCredentialRegistrationRequest  (
challenge  : challenge,   name  :   "  ada@example.com  "  ,   userID  : userHandle)
let   controller   =   ASAuthorizationController  (  authorizationRequests  : [request])
controller.  delegate   =   self
controller.  presentationContextProvider   =   self
controller.  performRequests  ()


// In the delegate:
if   let   reg   =   authorization.credential   as?   ASAuthorizationPlatformPublicKeyCredentialRegistration {
api.  finishRegistration  (  id  : reg.  credentialID  ,   clientData  : reg.  rawClientDataJSON  ,
attestation  : reg.  rawAttestationObject  )
}
```


On Android, add` androidx.credentials:credentials` and` androidx.credentials:credentials-play-services-auth` . The second is required on Android 13 and lower, as the[FIDO2 migration guide](https://developer.android.com/identity/sign-in/fido2-migration) explains. Take the current version from the[release notes](https://developer.android.com/jetpack/androidx/releases/credentials) . Then pass the server’s JSON straight to[CreatePublicKeyCredentialRequest](https://developer.android.com/identity/passkeys/create-passkeys) :


```text
val credentialManager   =   CredentialManager.  create  (context)
val result   =   credentialManager.  createCredential  (
context   =   activity,
request   =   CreatePublicKeyCredentialRequest  (requestJson   =   optionsJson)
) as CreatePublicKeyCredentialResponse
api.  finishRegistration  (result.registrationResponseJson)
```


The server then follows the[WebAuthn registration ceremony](https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-3/#sctn-registering-a-new-credential) . It checks the challenge, the origin and the rpId hash, then stores the credential ID, public key, sign count and user handle. Android apps send an origin of` android:apk-key-hash:<encoded SHA 256 fingerprint>` , and your server has to accept that exact value as one of its allowed origins. Add one origin per signing certificate.


## Sign-In: Assertion and Server Verification


Passkey sign-in follows the same pattern as registration. The server issues a challenge, the device signs it with the private key, and the server verifies the signature against the stored public key. The app never decides whether a passkey is valid.


```text
let   request   =   provider.  createCredentialAssertionRequest  (  challenge  : challenge)
// Delegate receives ASAuthorizationPlatformPublicKeyCredentialAssertion:
// credentialID, rawClientDataJSON, rawAuthenticatorData, signature, userID
```


```text
val request   =   GetCredentialRequest  (  listOf  (  GetPublicKeyCredentialOption  (requestJson   =   optionsJson)))
val result   =   credentialManager.  getCredential  (context   =   activity, request   =   request)
api.  finishSignIn  ((result.credential as PublicKeyCredential).authenticationResponseJson)
```


Following the[assertion verification steps](https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-3/#sctn-verifying-assertion) , the server:


1. Confirms the challenge matches one it issued and hasn’t been used.
2. Checks the origin against the allow-list, including every Android` apk-key-hash` origin.
3. Checks that` rpIdHash` equals the SHA-256 hash of your rpId.
4. Requires the user-present flag, plus user-verified if your policy demands it.
5. Verifies the signature with the stored public key.
6. Applies the sign-count rule. The spec compares counters only when the stored or received value is nonzero, so don’t reject a counter of zero.


## Syncing Turns Passkeys Into an Account-Recovery Question


Synced passkeys show up on devices that never signed in to your app. Passkeys saved to[Google Password Manager](https://codelabs.developers.google.com/credential-manager-api-for-android) follow the user’s Google account to their other signed-in Android devices, and[iCloud Keychain syncs them](https://support.apple.com/en-us/102195) across the user’s Apple devices. A user can buy a new phone, open your app and sign in straight away.


Passkey syncing has three consequences for account recovery:


- **Lost phone, not lost account.** When a device is lost, the passkey is still available on the user’s other devices.
- **The platform account is now part of your security boundary.** How safe the passkey for your domain is depends on the user’s Apple or Google account, including its two-factor and recovery checks.
- **Not everyone syncs.** Users with keychain sync turned off, a third-party provider or no Google account on the device can still lose their only credential.


Allow several passkeys per account, add a screen where users can see and revoke them, and keep an email or OTP recovery route. On a fresh device, a sign-in that falls back to a password despite a synced passkey usually points to an rpId or allow-list bug rather than the user declining.


## Fallback for Old Devices and Refusers


Keep password or OTP sign-in alongside passkeys at launch.[Native passkeys on Android](https://developer.android.com/identity/passkeys) need Android 9 (API level 28) or higher, and[using a third-party passkey provider](https://developer.android.com/identity/sign-in/fido2-migration) needs Android 14. Some users will decline the prompt no matter what device they have. Handle` NoCredentialException` and` ASAuthorizationError.canceled` by showing the existing login form, not an error.


Offer passkey creation after a successful password sign-in instead of forcing it at signup. Treat the older path as permanent until your data shows it can be demoted.[How passwordless login works](https://blog.openreplay.com/passwordless-login-works/) explains why passkeys hold up better than magic links and OTPs. React Native and Flutter apps follow the same rules: whatever bridge library you choose calls these same native APIs, so the association files and server checks don’t change.


## Conclusion


Most passkey bugs are configuration bugs, not code bugs. Before any native code, pick the rpId and host both association files at that exact domain. Check them with the two` curl` validators, and add the Play App Signing fingerprint and the Android origin to the server. Once both validators return your app, the Swift and Kotlin calls above are all the client code you need.


## FAQs


What minimum iOS version do passkeys need in a native app?


Synced passkeys need iOS 16 or later, the release where Apple introduced passkeys stored in iCloud Keychain. Credentials made with the built-in platform authenticator on iOS 15 or earlier never become passkeys and stay on the device that created them. To upgrade one, register a new credential with the same user handle, and iOS replaces the old credential with a synced passkey. On Android, the floor is Android 9 (API level 28).


Can users sign in to the app with a passkey they created on my website?


Yes, as long as the website and the app use the same rpId. A passkey is scoped to the rpId, not to the client, so one credential works in the browser and in both native apps. iOS native apps report an origin of https:// plus the rpId, the same value the website sends. Android apps report an android:apk-key-hash origin, which the server must add to its allow-list separately.


Can I test passkeys on the Android emulator and the iOS Simulator?


On Android, yes. Use an emulator image with Google Play (not plain AOSP) at API level 28 or higher, sign in with a Google account, and set a screen lock, because Google Password Manager stores the passkey. Without those, credential creation fails with an exception that looks like an app bug. The iOS Simulator can behave differently from real hardware, so run final passkey tests on a physical iPhone.


Which errors point to a broken association rather than a code bug?


On Android, CreatePublicKeyCredentialDomException during registration usually means assetlinks.json is missing or unreachable, lists the wrong package name or fingerprint, or sits on a host that does not match the rpId. On iOS, a broken association often shows up as ASAuthorizationError code 1001, the same code a user cancel produces. GetCredentialCancellationException on Android means the user dismissed the sheet and needs no error message.
